description: Four-panel composite of EBSD combined band-contrast / phase-identification maps of the same steel at increasing true strain: (a) 0.03, (b) 0.10, (c) 0.20, (d) 0.27, each with its own 5 µm scale bar (bottom-left) and a (a)-(d) label (top-left). The colour coding visible in the pixels is green for austenite, light-grey for ferrite and black for martensite (poor band contrast from high dislocation density); thin blue/cyan lines trace grain boundaries, with cyan-dominant boundaries interpreted as small-angle grain boundaries. Red rectangles mark blocky retained austenite (mostly at triple-junction boundaries) and red ellipses mark lath-like austenite between ferrite laths or inside ferrite grains. In (a) both blocky and lath-like austenite are abundant; blocky grains shrink in (b) and are nearly gone in (c); in (d) only small, sparse lath-like green patches remain and the panel is overprinted with the text "small angle grain boundaries" and two black arrows pointing at dense cyan boundary networks. The green area fraction decreases monotonically across (a)→(d), which is what makes the figure's argument: strain-induced martensitic (TRIP) transformation consumes retained austenite continuously, and the surviving austenite progressively changes from blocky to lath-like morphology while small-angle boundary density rises.

subfigures.description: EBSD band-contrast + phase map at true strain 0.03, 5 µm scale bar. Large green (austenite) regions dominate, including a blocky grain outlined by a red rectangle at a triple-junction boundary and lath-like austenite outlined by red ellipses. Light-grey ferrite matrix with black martensite areas; blue/cyan grain-boundary lines.

Same mapping at true strain 0.10, 5 µm scale bar. Green austenite fraction is visibly reduced; one red rectangle marks a remaining blocky austenite grain (upper right) and one red ellipse marks a thin lath-like austenite region. Grey ferrite grains contain small black/white dotted artefacts (unindexed or indexed points).

Same mapping at true strain 0.20, 5 µm scale bar. Green austenite occurs only as small isolated patches; one red rectangle and two red ellipses mark the few remaining austenite regions. Ferrite grains are larger and heavily subdivided by boundary lines; martensite (black) area increased.

Same mapping at true strain 0.27, 5 µm scale bar. Only sparse, small green austenite patches remain, highlighted by two red ellipses; the microstructure is dominated by grey ferrite and black martensite crossed by a dense network of cyan boundary lines. An overlaid white box reads "small angle grain boundaries" with two black arrows pointing to the cyan network.

observations.observation: The figure comprises four EBSD combined band-contrast and phase-identification maps of the same material at true strains 0.03 (a), 0.10 (b), 0.20 (c) and 0.27 (d), each carrying a 5 µm scale bar.
The green phase fraction decreases monotonically from panel (a) to panel (d), consistent with progressive consumption of austenite by deformation-induced martensitic transformation.
The caption states the maps are combined band contrast and phase identification maps under different true strain, with panel order (a) 0.03, (b) 0.10, (c) 0.20, (d) 0.27.
The citing text states austenite is marked green, ferrite gray and martensite black (poor band contrast due to high dislocation density).
The citing text reports calculated austenite volume fractions of 31.4%, 22.3%, 10.1% and 4.7% at true strains 0.03, 0.10, 0.20 and 0.27 respectively; these numbers are not printed on the image.

Red rectangles in (a)-(c) mark blocky retained austenite located at triple-junction boundaries; red ellipses mark lath-like austenite between ferrite laths or embedded in a single ferrite grain (per the citing text).
Blocky austenite grains that are large and outlined in (a) become rare by (c) and are essentially absent in (d), where the surviving green austenite is small and lath-like.
Panel (d) contains an overlaid text label "small angle grain boundaries" with two black arrows pointing to dense cyan/green boundary networks.

The citing text reports small-angle grain boundary fractions of 26%, 31%, 45% and 51% at true strains 0.03, 0.10, 0.20 and 0.27 respectively, with 51% at the largest strain; no such percentages appear on the panels.
Black, poorly indexed regions (martensite) visibly increase in area from (a) to (d) while grey ferrite grains become larger and more subdivided.
The citing text concludes that deformation-induced martensite transformation occurred continuously with increasing true strain, matching the trend in Fig. 3.
The EBSD analysis was performed on sample H90 at true strains of 0.03, 0.10, 0.20 and 0.27 to observe the TRIP effect.

unreadable_items: No numerical legend or colour-scale key is printed on any panel; the green/gray/black phase assignment comes only from the citing text
Individual grain-boundary misorientation values cannot be read from the maps; small-angle boundary fractions are only given in the text
Fine speckle/dotted texture inside some ferrite grains in (b) and (c) cannot be resolved confidently at the supplied resolution
